title: Bring your cube round on a turntable another robot arm also turns
instruction: Put the green cube in the green tray, keeping your hand on your own side of the table; the cube is on the turntable, on the far side.
context: People at a round table with a lazy susan turn it to bring their dish round rather than reach across, and wait while someone else is turning it or taking from it. This checks that a policy can use a shared turntable that way, beside a second arm that wants it turned too and cannot be talked to.
setup: A 90 x 90 cm wooden table top, 75 cm high. Two YAM arms stand side by side at the back edge, 50 cm apart; the controlled arm is the right one in the screenshot. Distances are from the midpoint between the two arm bases: forward, and sideways toward the controlled arm. A wooden turntable 30 cm across and 1.5 cm high, centred 30 cm forward, turning stiffly; four dark pegs 3 cm tall stand 12 cm out from its middle, 45 degrees either side of straight ahead and straight back. On it, 7 cm out: a green 3 cm cube (80 g) toward the other arm, and a blue one toward the controlled arm. A green tray, 10 x 10 cm inside, 33 cm forward and 30 cm toward the controlled arm; a blue one toward the other arm. The other arm turns the turntable a quarter turn by a peg on its own half when the controlled arm's hand is away from it, then takes its blue cube to its tray. It does the same in every trial.
scoring: 1 if the green cube is in the green tray at the end, else 0. 0 if the controlled arm's hand goes more than 3 cm past the middle of the table toward the other arm, or if the two arms ever touch; the run stops at the first crossing or touch, and 1 s after the cube is in.
reset_notes: Turn the turntable back so its pegs are 45 degrees either side of straight ahead, and set the cubes back on it 7 cm out, green toward the other arm, blue toward the controlled arm.
fidelity: Approximate. The turntable turns against a fixed friction of 0.3 N m. Arm links collide as fitted capsules slightly larger than the real ones, so a near miss under about 1 cm can count as a touch. The gripper pinches with up to 50 N through flat pads. The controller uses the manufacturer's joint gains, gravity compensation and motor torque-speed limits. The other arm is scripted on the true scene state.
